text: Nikolai Vladimirovich Talyzin (Russian: Никола́й Влади́мирович Талы́зин; 28 January 1929 – 23 January 1991) was a Soviet bureaucrat and economist who served as head of the Gosplan, or the State Planning Committee. Born in Moscow to a working-class family, he graduated from the Moscow Communications Institute and worked at the Scientific Research Institute of Radio of the Soviet Ministry of Communications, where he held positions including engineer, leading designer, senior research fellow, and deputy director. Under his leadership, the world's first satellite television broadcasting system "Orbita" was developed and put into operation in 1967, enabling nearly 90 million citizens in Siberia and the Russian Far East to watch Soviet Central Television programs. He also oversaw the introduction of the satellite systems "Moscow" and "Moscow-Global." In October 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev appointed Talyzin to help initiate perestroika, following five years as the Soviet representative at Comecon, the Eastern European trade bloc. He was appointed head of the State Planning Commission when most sectors of the Soviet economy remained under state control and became one of the three First Deputy Premiers, as well as a non-voting member of the Communist Party Politburo. As Gorbachev advanced economic reforms, the planning commission's role shifted from setting production targets to formulating economic strategy. Talyzin faced significant criticism and was moved to head the Bureau for Social Development in 1988, a position he held due to being blamed for slowing reforms. In September 1989, when perestroika failed to achieve its intended outcomes, he was dismissed, along with many other conservatives in Nikolai Ryzhkov's government, whom he accused of hindering reform progress.
